abstract: Neural system size is a fundamental quantitative property that may influence cognitive function. While larger neural systems have been associated with enhanced cognitive performance, how system size contributes to cognitive flexibility remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear whether size influences not only how efficiently a system learns but also how previously established neural dynamics are reorganized when learned associations must change. We addressed this question using recurrent neural networks trained on a reversal learning task. Despite reaching the same performance criterion, networks differed strikingly in how their internal dynamics changed across reversal. Some networks largely preserved prereversal population trajectories, thereby reusing previously established dynamics, whereas others substantially reorganized them, effectively reconstructing their dynamical structure. This continuum of adaptation strategies was particularly broad in small networks. Importantly, the extent of reorganization was related to network properties established before reversal: networks with larger prereversal recurrent weights tended to exhibit stronger reconstruction. We then examined whether the balance between reuse and reconstruction depended systematically on network size. As network size increased, changes in internal dynamics became progressively smaller and less variable, indicating increasing convergence toward the reuse strategy. Larger networks also learned both the initial and reversed mappings more rapidly and consistently. Thus, network size shapes not only learning efficiency but also the strategy by which previously learned population dynamics are modified during flexible adaptation, shifting the balance from diverse reuse reconstruction strategies in small networks toward consistent reuse in larger networks.
